cards.title: Reliability
cards.teaser: A reliable system continues to work correctly — at the right level of performance, under hardware faults, software bugs, and human mistakes — even when things go wrong. Reliability is not about perfection; it is about tolerating imperfection.

runs.text: Martin Kleppmann opens
Designing Data-Intensive Applications

with a deceptively simple claim: data systems must be reliable, scalable, and maintainable. Of the three, reliability is the most foundational — without it, the other two properties are pointless. A scalable system that loses data or produces wrong answers is not a system; it is a liability.
Kleppmann defines reliability through four expectations a user has of a system:

items.text: The application performs the function the user expected.
It can tolerate the user making mistakes or using the software in unexpected ways.
Its performance is good enough for the required use case, under expected load and data volume.
The system prevents any unauthorized access and abuse.

runs.text: The word
correctly

does the heavy lifting here. A system that returns stale data is not working correctly. A system that drops 0.1% of writes under high load is not working correctly. Reliability demands that the system honor its specification — not just most of the time, but consistently.

Reliability matters even for non-critical applications. If your personal finance app occasionally miscalculates your bank balance, or your photo app randomly deletes images, users lose trust permanently. The stakes vary; the expectation does not.

A reliable system keeps doing the right thing even when things go wrong — hardware crashes, bugs slip through, users do unexpected things. Reliability is about gracefully absorbing problems, not preventing them entirely.

cards.title: Fault vs Failure
cards.teaser: Kleppmann draws a precise line: a fault is a component deviating from its spec; a failure is the whole system stopping to provide the required service. Fault tolerance means preventing faults from cascading into failures — not eliminating faults.

runs.text: This distinction is one of the most important in the book. In ordinary conversation, "fault" and "failure" are synonyms. In distributed systems engineering, they are not.

items.text: Fault

— one component of the system deviates from its specification. A disk that returns corrupted bytes. A process that crashes. A network packet that gets dropped. A developer who introduced a bug. Faults are normal; they happen constantly in any large system.
Failure

— the system as a whole stops providing the required service to the user. The shopping cart returns 503. The database refuses writes. The payment processor times out for all requests. Failures are what users experience.

runs.text: The goal of fault-tolerant system design is to ensure that faults do not cascade into failures. A single disk dying should not bring down a database. A single node crashing should not make an API unavailable. A misconfigured feature flag should not corrupt user data.
Counterintuitively, Kleppmann argues that it can make sense to
increase

the rate of faults deliberately in order to ensure the fault-tolerance machinery is exercised and actually works. If the machinery is never triggered by real faults, you cannot be confident it will work when it is needed. This is the logic behind Netflix's
Chaos Monkey
: deliberately terminate random production instances to verify that the rest of the system absorbs the fault without failing.

Chasing zero faults is the wrong goal — it is impossible at scale. Designing systems that tolerate faults without failing is the right goal. The distinction shapes every architectural decision downstream.

A fault is something going wrong in one part of the system — a disk dies, a process crashes. A failure is what users see when the whole system stops working. The engineering challenge is to let faults happen without letting them become failures.

cards.title: Hardware, Software, and Human Fault Sources
cards.teaser: Faults come from three distinct sources — hardware failures, software bugs, and human errors — and each requires different mitigation strategies. Understanding the source determines whether redundancy, testing, or process controls is the right tool.

runs.text: Kleppmann categorizes faults into three distinct classes. The classification matters because each class has fundamentally different characteristics and mitigations.

items.text: Hardware faults.

Hard disks fail, RAM develops errors, power supplies die, network switches malfunction. These are random, largely independent events. A hard disk has a mean time to failure (MTTF) of roughly 10–50 years; in a cluster of 10,000 disks, you expect roughly one to fail per day. The standard mitigation is redundancy: RAID, dual power supplies, hot-standby servers. Hardware faults are well-understood and have mature solutions.
Software errors.

Systematic faults — a bug that causes every instance of a service to crash when it receives a certain input. A runaway process consuming all CPU or memory. A cascading failure triggered by a bad response from a dependency. Unlike hardware faults, software bugs are
correlated

— the same bug hits all nodes simultaneously. Redundancy provides no protection against a bug that crashes every replica at once. Mitigations include: careful design and testing, process isolation, allowing processes to crash and restart, measuring and monitoring system behavior in production.
Human errors.

Studies of large internet services have found that configuration errors by operators are the leading cause of outages. Humans are unreliable; even careful engineers make mistakes under pressure. Mitigations are multi-layered: well-designed abstractions that minimize opportunity for error, sandbox environments, thorough automated testing, easy rollback mechanisms, detailed monitoring and alerting, and good management practices.

runs.text: The relationship between the three classes is important: hardware faults are independent and random (one disk dies, others are fine); software bugs are correlated (one bug, all nodes affected); human errors are correlated and often latent (a misconfiguration sits dormant until the code path is exercised).

Human error is the hardest category to address because the solution is not technical. Kleppmann's recommendation — design systems so that errors are easy to detect, contain, and reverse — is essentially a UX principle applied to operator tooling.

Hardware faults are random and independent — add redundancy. Software bugs are correlated — add testing and sandboxing. Human errors are the sneakiest — design systems that make mistakes easy to detect and undo.

cards.title: Fault Tolerance
cards.teaser: Fault tolerance is the system property that allows it to continue operating correctly despite faults in its components — achieved through redundancy, isolation, and recovery mechanisms, and validated through deliberate fault injection.

runs.text: Fault-tolerant systems are built around a core insight: any component
will
fail eventually. The question is not whether to handle failure but how. Fault tolerance strategies fall into a few broad categories.

items.text: Redundancy.

Run multiple copies of every component. If one fails, others can take over. RAID arrays for disk failures. Multiple replicas for databases. Multi-AZ deployments for cloud services. The redundant copy absorbs the failure without service interruption.
Isolation.

Contain failures so they do not propagate. Process isolation via containers prevents a crashing service from consuming all memory on a host. Circuit breakers prevent a slow downstream dependency from causing all calling services to queue indefinitely. Bulkheads (a term from ship design) separate pools of resources so that exhausting one does not exhaust all.
Recovery.

Design for fast recovery when failures do occur. Processes that restart automatically. Checkpointing in stream processors so that progress is not lost on restart. Idempotent operations so that retrying a failed request produces the same result as a successful one.

runs.text: The most important validation technique is
Chaos Engineering
— deliberately injecting faults in production (or production-like environments) to verify that the fault-tolerance mechanisms actually work. Netflix pioneered this with
Chaos Monkey
(random instance termination) and later expanded it to the
Simian Army
: tools that simulate network latency (
Latency Monkey
), entire availability zone failures (
Chaos Gorilla
), and more. Chaos Engineering does not make systems more reliable — it reveals which parts are not as reliable as assumed.

Fault tolerance machinery that is never exercised in production is fault tolerance machinery that may not work in production. Chaos Engineering is the discipline that closes this gap by making fault injection a regular, scheduled practice rather than an accident.

Fault tolerance means the system keeps working when parts of it break. You achieve it by duplicating components, isolating failures, and recovering quickly. You validate it by intentionally breaking things in production with tools like Chaos Monkey.

cards.title: Scalability
cards.teaser: Scalability describes a system's ability to cope with increased load — but "increased load" is meaningless without a precise definition of what load means for your specific system. Scalability begins with measurement, not with architecture.

runs.text: Kleppmann is careful to point out that scalability is not a one-dimensional property of a system. You cannot say "Twitter is scalable" any more than you can say "Twitter is tall." The question is always:
scalable with respect to what?
Scalable for what kind of load growth? Along what axis?

Kleppmann's definition: scalability is the term we use to describe a system's ability to cope with increased load. More precisely, it is about having strategies for keeping performance good as load increases. The key word is
strategies
— scalability is not a binary property but a set of deliberate choices about how to add resources when load grows.
The scalability conversation has two parts:

items.text: Describing load precisely.
What are the load parameters for your system? You cannot reason about scaling without naming them. (See: Load Parameters, next card.)
Describing performance under load.
If load doubles, what happens to performance? Do you need to double hardware to maintain performance? Does performance degrade gracefully or catastrophically? Which operations are affected?

runs.text: These two questions — what is load, and what does performance look like as load changes — are the foundation of any scalability analysis. Systems that skip this analysis and jump directly to "add more nodes" often find that their bottleneck was not what they assumed.
Scalability is about handling growth in load without degrading. But you have to define what "load" means for your system before you can reason about whether you can handle more of it.

cards.title: Load Parameters
cards.teaser: Load parameters are the numbers that describe how much work your system is doing — and picking the right metric is an architectural decision, not a reporting decision. Twitter's architecture changed when it chose the right one.

runs.text: Load can be described in different ways depending on the system. The right
load parameters

for a web server might be requests per second. For a database, it might be the ratio of reads to writes. For a cache, it might be the hit rate. For a stream processor, it might be the number of messages being processed per second, plus the lag between message arrival and processing.
Kleppmann uses the
Twitter home timeline
as the canonical example, because it illustrates that there is rarely one obvious load parameter — and that the right choice has profound architectural consequences.
Twitter's two main operations:

items.text: Post tweet:
a user publishes a new tweet (~4.6k requests/second on average, ~12k at peak).
Home timeline:
a user wants to see tweets from people they follow (~300k requests/second).

runs.text: Twitter tried two approaches.
Approach 1

: on each timeline request, do a SQL join — find all the people the user follows, fetch their recent tweets, merge and sort. This works at low scale but the home timeline query becomes expensive as follow graphs grow.
Approach 2

: when a user posts a tweet, fan out and write that tweet into the home timeline cache of every follower. Timeline reads become cheap (just read a pre-computed cache). But for a user with 30 million followers, one tweet means 30 million writes.
Twitter's key insight: the load parameter that mattered was
the distribution of followers per user

— specifically the existence of celebrity accounts. Twitter ultimately moved to a hybrid: most users use the fan-out approach, but celebrities with massive follower counts are handled differently to avoid the write amplification. The load parameter drove the architecture.

Picking the right load parameter is not obvious. It requires understanding which aspect of load will actually stress the system — and that often requires real production data rather than pre-launch guesses.

Load parameters are the numbers that capture how hard your system is working. Pick the wrong one and you optimize for the wrong thing. Twitter's home timeline architecture changed completely when engineers focused on "followers per user" rather than just "tweets per second".

cards.title: Throughput
cards.teaser: Throughput measures how much work a system can do per unit of time — records processed per second, bytes written per second, transactions committed per second. It is a measure of capacity, not experience, and it describes a different axis than response time.

runs.text: Throughput and response time are often confused but they measure different things:

items.text: Throughput
— the number of records a system can process per second, or the total time it takes to run a job on a dataset of a given size. It is a capacity measure: how much work can the system do?
Response time
— the time between a client sending a request and receiving a response. It is an experience measure: how long does a user wait?

runs.text: Kleppmann notes that in
batch processing
systems (like Hadoop), throughput is often the key metric — you care about processing 10 billion records in 4 hours, not about how long any individual record takes. In
online systems
(web services, databases), response time is the primary measure of user experience. Most real-world systems care about both, but they trade off differently depending on the workload.
The relationship between throughput and response time is governed by Little's Law:
L = λW

— the average number of requests in a system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average time spent in the system. If response time (W) increases because of queuing, and the arrival rate (λ) stays constant, the system grows deeper queues (L). Throughput is bounded by the slowest component in the chain.

Throughput is the right primary metric when you have a large fixed dataset to process and the job's total time matters (batch ETL, analytics, ML training). Response time is the right primary metric when users are waiting for individual responses (APIs, OLTP databases, search).

Throughput is how much work the system can do per second — a batch job processing 1 million records per second. Response time is how long a single user waits for a reply. They are related but measure different things, and optimizing one does not automatically optimize the other.

cards.title: Response Time vs Latency
cards.teaser: Response time and latency are not synonyms. Kleppmann's distinction: response time is what the client measures — service time plus network delay plus queuing. Latency is the duration a request spends waiting to be handled, before processing begins.

runs.text: The conflation of response time and latency is pervasive in engineering discussions, and it matters because they implicate different remediation strategies.

items.text: Response time

— what the client measures from when it sends a request to when it receives the full response. It includes: actual service time (processing the request), network delay (transmitting bytes in both directions), and queuing delay (time the request spent waiting for a server to become available). Response time is the end-to-end experience.
Latency
— the duration a request is
latent

, meaning awaiting service rather than being actively processed. Strictly, latency is queuing delay: the time between a request arriving at the server and the moment processing begins. In practice, engineers often use "latency" loosely to mean response time.

runs.text: Kleppmann explicitly notes this ambiguity: "Latency and response time are often used synonymously, but they are not the same thing." He recommends using
response time
when you mean what the client observes, and
latency
when you mean waiting time specifically.

Why it matters in practice: a response time spike could be caused by a slow service (fix the code), network congestion (fix the infrastructure), or queuing at an overloaded server (fix the capacity). Diagnosing correctly requires knowing which component is contributing most. Measuring response time end-to-end tells you there is a problem; tracing the breakdown tells you where.

Response time is the total time from sending a request to getting the reply — it includes processing, network, and waiting in queue. Latency, strictly speaking, is just the waiting-in-queue part. Engineers use both terms loosely, but knowing the difference helps you find the root cause when things are slow.

cards.title: Response Time Percentiles
cards.teaser: The average response time is a lie. It hides the users who are experiencing the worst performance. Percentiles — p50, p95, p99, p999 — tell you what the slowest users actually experience, and that is what determines whether your SLO is met.

runs.text: If you make 100 requests to a service and measure the response time of each, you have a distribution. The mean collapses that distribution into a single number that may accurately describe no individual request. Percentiles preserve the shape of the distribution.

items.text: p50 (median)
— 50% of requests were faster than this. The "typical" request. If p50 is 100ms, half your users see under 100ms.
— 95% of requests were faster than this. 5% of users experience something worse.
— 99% of requests were faster. 1 in 100 users sees something worse.
— 99.9% of requests were faster. 1 in 1,000 users sees something worse. At 10,000 requests per second, that is 10 users per second hitting a terrible experience.

runs.text: Kleppmann explains why averages mislead with a concrete example: if most requests take 10ms but 1% take 10 seconds, the mean might be 110ms — a number that accurately describes neither the fast majority nor the slow tail. The mean obscures the users having a bad experience.

Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and Service Level Agreements (SLAs) are almost always expressed in percentiles for this reason. An SLA might say: "response time will be below 200ms at p99." Amazon, Google, and Netflix all define their reliability commitments this way, not as averages.
High percentiles (
) are called
tail latencies

. Kleppmann notes that Amazon describes response time requirements for internal services in the 99.9th percentile, even though this only affects 1 in 1,000 requests, because the customers with the slowest requests often have the most data and are therefore the most valuable customers.
Never report average response time in dashboards. Always show p50, p95, and p99 at minimum. Averages create false confidence: a system with a 50ms mean and a 30-second p99 is not a 50ms system.

Percentiles tell you the response time for the slowest 1%, 5%, or 0.1% of users — the people most likely to abandon or complain. Averages hide them. SLAs and dashboards should always use percentiles, never means.

cards.title: Tail Latency and Head-of-Line Blocking
cards.teaser: Tail latency — the worst-case response times in a distribution — can be amplified by a subtle effect called head-of-line blocking: a single slow request holds up all subsequent requests behind it, turning one slow operation into many.

runs.text: Tail latency (high-percentile response times like
and

) is expensive to optimize because its causes are often rare and hard to reproduce. Common causes include: a garbage collection pause, a cache miss requiring a disk read, a context switch, a TCP retransmit, or a lock contention event.
Head-of-line blocking

amplifies tail latency. Consider a server processing requests in order. If request #5 is slow — a cache miss, a GC pause — requests #6, #7, #8, and all subsequent requests queue behind it. From the client's perspective, fast requests appear slow because they are stuck in line behind a slow one. Even though the server is capable of fast responses, the response time distribution degrades across the board.
This is why
queueing theory

matters in system design. Even with low average utilization, a single slow request can create a queue that raises the apparent response time of many subsequent fast requests. The effect is particularly visible in services that process requests in a small thread pool.
Tail latency compounds in distributed systems. If a user request requires calls to 5 backend services, the total response time is dominated by the slowest of the 5 — not the average. A
of 1 second on each backend service produces a
of 5 seconds at the end-to-end level if calls are sequential. Even parallel fan-out does not fully escape this: the slowest call determines the total time.

Kleppmann's advice: when benchmarking, keep sending requests at a fixed rate regardless of outstanding responses, so that queuing effects are visible in the measurement. An "artificial" benchmark that waits for each response before sending the next will underestimate head-of-line blocking.

Head-of-line blocking means one slow request makes everything behind it slow too. In distributed systems this compounds: if you make 5 parallel calls and one is slow, you wait for the slowest one, so your p99 is determined by the worst case across all your dependencies.

cards.title: Scaling Up vs Scaling Out
cards.teaser: Scaling up (vertical) means buying a bigger machine; scaling out (horizontal) means adding more machines and distributing the load. Modern architectures prefer horizontal scaling for its elasticity — but shared-nothing architecture is the prerequisite that makes it feasible.

runs.text: The two approaches to handling increased load:

items.text: Scaling up (vertical scaling).

Move to a machine with more CPUs, more RAM, faster disks. Simple — no change to the software architecture required. But it has a ceiling: the biggest available machine has finite capacity, and premium hardware gets disproportionately expensive as you approach the ceiling. It is also a single point of failure.
Scaling out (horizontal scaling).

Distribute load across many smaller machines. Each additional machine adds capacity linearly (in theory). There is no ceiling imposed by hardware — you can keep adding nodes. But it requires software designed for distribution: you must deal with partial failures, network communication, data partitioning, and consistency across nodes.

runs.text: Kleppmann notes that the choice is not binary. Many systems use a mix: scale up to a reasonable size first (easy wins), then scale out when needed. The economics often favor scale-up for moderate workloads and scale-out for very large ones.
Horizontal scaling requires a
shared-nothing architecture

— each node operates independently without requiring a shared resource (no shared disk, no shared memory, no shared coordinator). Shared-nothing systems are the basis of modern distributed databases like Cassandra, DynamoDB, and CockroachDB. Each node can be added or removed without a global coordination step.
Elasticity

is the property of scaling out automatically in response to load, and scaling back in when load decreases. Cloud platforms enable elastic scaling for stateless services easily; scaling stateful services (databases, queues) elastically is significantly harder because data must be redistributed when nodes are added or removed.

Shared-nothing architecture is powerful but demands more from the application layer. Distributed transactions, global ordering, and cross-node joins all become expensive or impossible. Every distributed system design is a negotiation between the benefits of horizontal scale and the complexity of distribution.

Scaling up means getting a bigger machine; scaling out means getting more machines. Scaling out is more flexible but requires that your software is designed to run across many nodes without sharing state — that is what shared-nothing architecture means.

cards.title: Operability
cards.teaser: Operability is the quality of a system that makes it easy for the operations team to keep it running smoothly — and it is as much a design goal as correctness. A brilliant system that nobody knows how to operate is not production-ready.

runs.text: Kleppmann quotes a concise definition from Kiciman and Fox: "good operations can often work around the limitations of bad (or incomplete) software, but good software cannot run reliably with bad operations." Operability is the system property that lets good operations flourish.
What operations teams actually do with a data system:

items.text: Monitor the health of the system and quickly restore service if it goes into a bad state.
Track down the cause of problems, such as system failures and degraded performance.
Keep software and platforms up to date, including security patches.
Keep tabs on how different systems affect each other so that a change to one does not cause problems in another.
Anticipate future problems and solve them before they occur (capacity planning).
Define processes that make operations predictable and help keep the production environment stable.

runs.text: Good operability means a system actively supports these tasks. Concretely:

items.text: Providing visibility into the runtime behavior and internals of the system with good monitoring.
Providing good support for automation and integration with standard tools.
Avoiding dependency on individual machines (no pets, only cattle).
Providing good documentation and an easy-to-understand operational model.
Providing good default behavior and giving administrators the freedom to override defaults when needed.
Behaving predictably to minimize surprises.

runs.text: Operability is often an afterthought — developers build the happy path and leave operations to figure out the rest. Kleppmann's framing makes it a first-class design goal, on par with reliability and scalability.

Operability means the system is designed to be easy to run in production — with good monitoring, predictable behavior, clear documentation, and support for automation. No matter how elegant the internals, a system that the operations team cannot safely manage is not production-ready.

cards.title: Simplicity
cards.teaser: Complexity is the enemy of reliability and maintainability — it makes systems hard to understand, hard to change, and easy to break in unexpected ways. Simplicity is not about having fewer features; it is about managing accidental complexity through abstraction.

runs.text: Kleppmann distinguishes between two kinds of complexity:

items.text: Essential complexity

— inherent in the problem itself. Distributed consensus is genuinely hard. Real-time fraud detection under high write volume is genuinely hard. This complexity cannot be removed without removing the functionality.
Accidental complexity

— complexity that arises from implementation choices, not from the problem domain. Tangled state, inconsistent APIs, hidden side effects, tight coupling between components. This complexity can and should be removed.

runs.text: The best tool for managing complexity is
abstraction

. A good abstraction hides a great deal of implementation detail behind a clean, simple facade. SQL is an abstraction over B-trees, buffer pools, and WAL logs — you do not need to understand any of that to write a query. TCP is an abstraction over packet switching, checksums, and retransmission — you just write to a socket.

The challenge: finding good abstractions is hard. Kleppmann notes that while the software engineering community has developed good general-purpose abstractions for programming languages and algorithms, there is still much less clarity about what good abstractions for distributed data systems look like. That is part of what the book is exploring.
Symptoms of accidental complexity in data systems:

items.text: Explosion of state space — too many moving parts, too many special cases.
Tight coupling — a change in one component requires changes in many others.
Tangled dependencies — you cannot understand component A without understanding B, C, and D.
Inconsistent naming and behavior — similar operations behave differently in different contexts.

runs.text: Moseley and Marks in "Out of the Tarpit" (2006) argue that complexity is the single greatest impediment to the development and maintenance of large-scale software systems. Kleppmann's treatment of simplicity in data systems echoes this: a complex system is hard to reason about, hard to test, and hard to change safely.

Simplicity in a data system does not mean fewer features. It means removing accidental complexity — the kind that comes from bad design choices, not from the problem itself. Good abstractions hide the messy parts and let you reason about the system at a higher level.

cards.title: Evolvability
cards.teaser: Evolvability — the ease with which a system can be adapted as requirements change — is the maintainability property most specific to data systems. Data outlives the code that wrote it, and that creates a long tail of schema evolution and backward compatibility obligations.

runs.text: Requirements change. New use cases emerge. Previously wrong assumptions become apparent. Business priorities shift. Legal requirements are updated. These are not failures of planning — they are the normal life cycle of any software system that is actually being used. A system's
evolvability
determines how expensive change will be.

In application code, evolvability corresponds to the agile practices that enable iterative development: simple design, refactoring, TDD, loosely coupled modules. Kleppmann argues that data systems have an additional dimension that application code does not:
data outlives the code that wrote it

If you change the code, you can redeploy immediately. But if you have 10 billion records written in the old schema format, you cannot change the schema without a migration. That migration may take hours or days to run. While it is running, you need to support both old and new code paths. After it runs, old clients that still produce old-format data will break.
This creates two compatibility constraints that data systems must manage:

items.text: Backward compatibility
— newer code can read data written by older code. Necessary during rolling deployments: new code is on some nodes, old code on others.
Forward compatibility
— older code can read data written by newer code. Harder to achieve, but required when old clients remain in the field (mobile apps, IoT devices, external partners).

runs.text: Evolvability in data systems is enabled by choosing data formats and encodings that support schema evolution gracefully — Avro, Protocol Buffers, and Thrift are all designed with this in mind. It is also enabled by designing systems with clear separation between the read and write paths (CQRS), between storage and computation, and between internal and external interfaces.

Kleppmann frames evolvability as "agility at the data layer." While application code can be refactored quickly, data systems require careful, disciplined evolution because the consequences of a bad schema migration can persist for years in stored records.

Evolvability means: how easy is it to change the system when requirements change? For data systems, this is harder than for code because data persists — you cannot just redeploy your way out of a schema mismatch. Good data formats and clean architecture boundaries are what make evolution manageable.
